# 7. Anuttara · Śakti · Māyā · the eye · veil · frame · horizon — finite sight and the forgotten condition

**Office:** deep-bearing authored cross-source Mytheme/image; linear-bearing joins into §0, §4 and the World-Picture → World-Atlas / Return fields. This is **not one inherited myth** and should never be presented as though Śaiva, Jungian and Gebserian sources told one historical narrative.

`[[inherited-corpus-crosswalk/01-DIFFERENTIATING-MIND|§0 — Differentiating Mind — Inherited Region Recovery]]` **grounds** the tattvic contraction; `[[inherited-corpus-crosswalk/05-PSYCHOID-FLOWERING|§4 — Psychoid Flowering — Inherited Region Recovery]]` **defines** the mature perspective/complex/diaphaneity pressure; `[[inherited-corpus-crosswalk/00-INTEGRAL-THRESHOLD|§0/1 — Integral Threshold — Inherited Region Recovery]]` **grounds** the formal limit; `[[THREAD-INTAKE-WHOLE-RELATIONAL-UNITS#Intake 001 — Self-Identity · Limit · Objective Internality · Confession · World|Intake 001]]` **extends** it through hybris, confession, nested internality and direct contemplative return.

## The whole image: seeing requires a hidden side

Begin with the eye, not as a detached biological organ but as an image of situated disclosure. To see anything at all, something must stand forth from something else. There must be orientation, foreground and background, a field from which this form is selected, a position from which it is seen and limits beyond which the present seeing does not reach. The eye's power depends upon conditions that do not appear inside its present picture in the same way as the object it sees.

That is the first and necessary concealment. **The condition of seeing is not simply another visible item omitted by accident.** If every condition of the perspective had to appear as another object inside that same perspective, a further perspective would already be presupposed from which the expanded field was given. The blind side belongs to finite seeing as finite seeing.

The Śaiva relation gives this image its metaphysical depth. **Anuttara/Paramaśiva** carries the unbounded or unobjectifiable ground; **Śakti** is the power of manifestation and self-articulation; **Māyā** is the threshold at which measure, subject/object difference and bounded determination become operative; the **kañcukas** contract universal powers into finite ratios of knowledge, efficacy, desire, time and ordering; **paśu** is the bounded subject-position inhabiting the resulting world; the inner instrument and its inherited scripts, memories, affects, images and valuations make that world practically available.

The veil is therefore not a foreign cloth thrown over an otherwise complete spectator. **The veil is the positive power by which a finite aperture can exist.** The same manifestation that makes a world visible withholds the whole from appearing as one more thing inside that world. Source is absent as exhaustive content while remaining present as condition.

This is why the current project must distinguish **constitutive self-veiling from hybris**. If manifestation is Līlā/play, the play requires real local positions, real appearances, real others and real consequences. A world in which every finite centre explicitly possessed the whole as content would have no genuine local disclosure through which encounter and recognition could occur.

## The second forgetting: hybris

The necessary blind side becomes pathological only when the finite measure forgets that it is finite.

```text
Māyā / contraction
  makes a bounded measure and world possible
        ↓
perspective
  discloses a real sector from a real position
        ↓
world-picture
  stabilises what that position can see and say
        ↓
hybris
  lets the frame perform as the horizon of Being
```

This is the mental-rational doubling of faults in its strongest form. Perspective earns extraordinary powers of comparison, objectification, geometry, criticism and exact measure by making a disciplined cut. The cut then disappears behind what it makes visible. Finally the success of the cut is used as evidence that what the cut cannot contain is unreal.

**A necessary methodological blindness becomes an unnecessary metaphysical blindness.**

The local `x` behaves as `X`; a pratibimba behaves as Bimba; the `1` occupies `0`; a finite ecology of measure silently installs its own source-position as the view from nowhere. The rational account then carries an irrational, repressed premise at its centre: *the jurisdiction of my measure is the jurisdiction of reality itself*.

This is the exact sense in which the frame mistakes its frame for the horizon of Being.

## Disregard and regard — the Other at the edge of the frame

The image becomes relational when another living centre stands where the current frame cannot already contain it.

The first response can be **disregard**. The frame does not literally fail to look; it looks *through an already completed measure*. The other is assigned a category, score, image, diagnosis, number, role or explanation before encounter has been allowed to modify the terms of judgment. The current account keeps its coherence by fitting the witness to itself.

This is why the Job friends, Apollo before Daphne, the Village before Number Six, the complex before new experience and the hidden evaluator before an affected world belong to the same larger seam without becoming the same story. In each, a real local measure can become an arbiter which no longer receives return from what it measures.

**Regard** names the contrary movement now earned by this thread: **turn toward what exceeds the present measure far enough that the encounter can modify the measure by which it was approached.** Regard is not suspension of judgment forever. It is the condition under which judgment remains intelligent because its criterion remains answerable to what it claims to judge.

This makes regard an ethical face of `[[submission-package/essay/section-rooms/arguments/08-deferential-intelligence|Deferential Intelligence]]` and of `[[submission-package/essay/symbolon/episteme/concepts/compassion-as-sensitivity-to-origins|Compassion as Sensitivity to Origins]]`. The latter already names the return as loving attention to genesis, exclusion, wound, purpose and affected Other. Followed deeply enough, sensitivity to origin releases a present determination from the fiction that it generated itself.

## Gebser: `180° → 360°` without a God's-eye view

The Gebser relation is essential and must remain at its mature resolution. `180°` names the perspectival achievement as a situated angular cut: a powerful view whose conditions of projection can disappear behind what it renders. `360°` does **not** mean that one observer becomes omniscient. It names the construction of **con-text**: the woven co-presence of positions, transitions, conditions, occlusions and counter-orientations through which no single perspective is permitted to impersonate the field.

One perspective cannot complete itself merely by becoming wider. What it lacks is positively borne by positions it cannot occupy at once. Counter-perspective is therefore productive. At least two genuinely differentiated orientations can disclose the conditions each cannot generate from inside itself; a richer contextual field can then carry their relation without reducing one to the other.

```text
perspective / text
        ↓ meets
counter-perspective / other text
        ↓
con-text
  the views and the conditions of their viewing are woven together
        ↓
diaphaneity
  origin shines through finite form without becoming another final view
```

This is the integral `complexio oppositorum` operation in epistemic form. **Integral does not mean the perspective that contains all perspectives.** That would repeat Mental-Rational hybris at a higher altitude. Integral means that situated perspectives become mutually and historically transparent inside a field no one view owns.

## Jung: ego, complex, Self and the horizon of the unconscious

The same whole refracts psychologically. The ego is a real local centre of orientation; persona, complex, self-image and inherited cultural scripts are real organised formations. They become pathological when one local formation performs as the determining whole and its valuation regime becomes invisible.

`[[inherited-corpus-crosswalk/05-PSYCHOID-FLOWERING|§4 recovery]]` already describes the complex as a locally stabilised arbitration/valuation basin: some cues become disproportionately salient, some responses arrive pre-weighted and a once-adaptive position can reappear as though it were the whole situation. **Individuation is de-monopolisation**, not destruction of the ego. The local centre becomes more definite while its relation to the wider determining field becomes more transparent.

The unconscious can therefore be read, at this project level, as what lies beyond the current ego's event horizon: psychic, somatic, collective, archetypal and environmental conditions that affect the local centre without being exhausted by its present representation. Jung's Self is not thereby reduced to “everything the ego does not know”; it supplies the wider ordering problem through which the ego can be relativised without being annulled.

Job gives this psychological operation its theological violence. A protected God-image is forced into answerability by what it cannot assimilate. Apollo/Daphne gives it its erotic image. The ouroboros/torus gives it topology. Gebser gives it historical consciousness.

## Anamnesis / Pratyabhijñā — remembering what was hidden as condition

The return is not the acquisition of one final object called “the Absolute.” It is recognition **within determination** of the condition that determination could not carry as ordinary determinate content.

This gives Plato's *anamnesis* and Śaiva *pratyabhijñā* an exact project-level operational meeting while their historical doctrines remain separate:

```text
source becomes implicit in finite manifestation
        ↓
determination lives as real local world
        ↓
its ground is forgotten as ground
        ↓
limit / contradiction / Other interrupts closure
        ↓
recognition remembers relation
        ↓
finite form remains, now transparent to source
```

The compact mature formulation is:

> **Māyā limits. Perspective delineates. Hybris absolutises. Regard reopens. Recognition returns.**

Or at the mythic/metaphysical register:

> **Līlā veils; hybris absolutises the veil; recognition sees the veil as Śakti.**

These are authorial compressions derived from the whole above, not source quotations.

## What full recovery changes

This whole prevents a major conceptual error: treating limitation, perspective, Māyā or rational determination themselves as the enemy. The world is possible because difference becomes real enough to have a point of view. **The fall is not the existence of the frame; the fall is the frame forgetting that it is framed.**

That distinction also gives the essay a stronger account of why the limiting condition tends to be forgotten. The condition withdraws from ordinary content *because it is functioning as condition*. The eye does not see its seeing in the same way it sees the seen. A world-picture can therefore forget its own picture-making without anybody choosing a metaphysical doctrine. Hybris is the secondary closure that turns this constitutive blind side into sovereign certainty.

For native 018 / #39, this whole should control any later separation of Māyā-as-measure, Hybris, Perspective, Context, Diaphaneity, Regard and Recognition into distinct nodes. They are not a prose list. They are moments inside one whole movement of finite disclosure, closure, encounter and return.

**Source debt:** direct Trika/Pratyabhijñā source depth for Māyā, contraction, Līlā/self-veiling and recognition; exact Gebser source control for perspective, aperspectivity/diaphaneity and ever-present Origin; Jung source control for ego/Self/individuation and the relevant historical/aionic claims; Plato source work for anamnesis; and a separate etymological archaeology of regard/disregard and hybris. The theoretical yield remains authorial where those source claims are not yet installed.

### 12. Stained glass: constructing from diaphaneity

The stained-glass image gives this methodology a fuller body than “mosaic” alone. A mosaic assembles opaque fragments into a surface image. Stained glass does something more: it constructs with the transmission, refraction, colouring, and obstruction of light. Its material joins are as important as its luminous panes.

In the image's metaphysical register, light can refract Prakāśa: the luminosity by which anything appears. The coloured panes are traditions, disciplines, concepts, experiences, and media. Their colour is not an impurity to be removed in pursuit of colourless neutrality; it is the determinate power by which otherwise ungraspable light becomes visible in a particular form. The lead cames are the seams QL/MEF refuses to erase: provenance, non-equivalence, historical difference, evidential limit, contradiction, translation, and the exact boundary at which one register yields to another. Without the seams there is no articulated window. Without transmitted light there is only an inventory of coloured matter.

The image appears neither in the light alone nor in the panes alone. It arises through their relation, for a viewer situated on one side of the constructed aperture. Move the sun, the viewer, or the angle and a different intensity enters the room; the pattern remains recognisable while its living appearance changes. This is an exact image of a context that is real, constructed, and revisable. The window does not invent the light, and it does not transmit an unconditioned view. It builds a form through which origin can become diaphanous.

“Constructing from diaphaneity” begins while the argument's materials are chosen and joined according to how they transmit, bend, colour, interrupt, and recompose the originating movement. Diaphaneity becomes an architectural principle. A source enters the work as a pane whose exact refractive operation changes the visible whole; a tile used only to prove that a position has many supporters would perform a different and far weaker office. The joins remain visible so that the reader can tell where light passed through Jung, through Abhinavagupta, through a mathematical derivation, through an anomalous experience, or through a designed agentic experiment.

The torus adds a complementary mytheme. It is individuated as a coherent surface precisely by retaining its hole. Its apparent wound is not an injury later repaired; the gap gives the form its genus and permits non-contractible circulation. An infinite field can express local indivisibility in the same way: not by filling every gap or erasing every distinction, but by forming a coherent circulation around a centre it cannot objectify. The stained-glass window and the torus meet here. One makes the unseen source visible through differential transmission; the other makes a whole by preserving the unfilled centre through which return remains possible.

These are governing images, not literal equations. Prakāśa is not electromagnetic radiation; a tradition is not physically a coloured pane; individuation is not topological genus. Their validity lies in the operations they make visible after the formal and historical relations have been separately established.

### 13. From 180-degree perspective to 360-degree context

The Gebser movement becomes precise when joined to the QL passage from #3 Pattern to #4 Context. A perspective selects a view from a situated point. It gains extraordinary clarity by projecting a field into ordered relations, but the conditions of projection tend to disappear behind what the perspective makes visible. In the project's geometric development, the triangle's 180 degrees carries the three sequential persons or positions; the square's 360 degrees holds them together as a contextual field.

The 360-degree turn achieves contextual co-presence while every observer remains situated within a horizon. It changes the unit of understanding from *which view is correct?* to *what field makes these views possible, how do they transform one another, what does each disclose or occlude, and what appears only through their co-presence?* Context is the organised availability of positions, transitions, conditions, and limits; its completeness belongs to their relation and remains different from a final panoramic picture.

This is why the essay's integral method must construct context. A context is not a neutral background already waiting to be described. It is an achieved world in which sources can answer one another without losing their own laws; in which mathematical, phenomenological, psychological, metaphysical, historical, empirical, and technical claims retain their registers; and in which the reader can move among them while seeing why each is placed where it is. The movement from perspective to context is therefore also the movement from isolated agent to agentic cosmos. In both cases the primary object ceases to be a bounded view or bounded actor and becomes the field of relations through which views and actors acquire determinate force.

# The Doctrine of Vibration - An Analysis of the Doctrines and Practices of Kashmir Shaivism
## By Mark S.G. Dyczkowski

### Pages 60-85: Prakāśa (Light of Consciousness) and Spanda (Universal Activity)

---

## Page 60: Prakāśa: The Light of Consciousness

*Prakāśa* is the pure 'luminosity' (*bhāsa*) or 'self-showing' that constitutes the essence and ultimate identity (*ātman*) of phenomena. That things appear at all is due to the light of consciousness, and their appearing (*avabhāsana*) is itself this Light which bestows on all things their evident, manifest nature. Established in the light of consciousness everything appears there according to its own specific nature (*svabhāva*). Anything that supposedly does not rest in this Light is as unreal as a sky-flower. Thus, according to Rājānaka Rāma, unlike the light of the sun, or any other light, this Light not only makes all things apparent, it is also their ultimate source. Full of its divine vibration the Light makes all things manifest and withdraws them into itself. This supra-temporal activity characterises it most specifically; devoid of it, it would be no better than an inert physical phenomenon. At the same time, this light is the conjunction (*śleṣa*) or oneness (*aikātmya*) of its countless manifest forms, and the collective whole (*sampindana*) of all the categories of existence. The universe is nothing but the shining of the Light within itself. It is the radiant vibration (*sphurattā*) of this Light, the state (*avasthāna*) in which consciousness becomes manifest.

Although the Light shines as all things at all times and hence also makes their diversity manifest, penetrating each object individually as well as collectively, it is not totally 'merged' (*magna*) or identified with the object so as to suffer any division within itself. Our experience of any object is of the form: 'I see this': it is not itself an object, but the manifest form the object assumes as a luminous principle of experience. The Light is ever revealed and can never be obscured; objectivity can never cast a shadow on the light of consciousness. The *Stanzas on Vibration* declare:

> That in which all this creation is established and from whence it arises is nowhere obstructed because it is unconditioned by [its very] nature.

This Light is the highest reality (*paramārtha*). It is the 'Ancient Light' (*pūrvaprakāśa*) that makes all things new and fresh every moment. It is 'always new and secret, ancient and known to all.' It is the form of the Present (*vartamānarūpa*), the Eternal Now. Time and space are relations between the contents of consciousness; they cannot impinge on the integrity of the absolute itself. Neither space nor time can divide it, for they are one with the Light that illumines them and makes them known as elements of experience. But this Light is the shining of the absolute, it is not an impersonal principle. It is the living Light of God, indeed it is God Himself, the Master Who instructs the entire universe. Śiva is this 'auspicious lamp', Who illumines all things. He is the Light of consciousness that reveals the presence of both the real and the unreal, of 'light' and 'darkness'. Abhinavagupta writes:

---

## Page 61: Light and Awareness: Two Aspects of Consciousness

Thus Bhairava, the Light, is self-evident (*svataḥsiddha*); without beginning. He is the first and last of all things, the Eternal Present. And so what else can be said of Him? The unfolding of the categories of existence (*tattva*) and creation, which are the expansion of His own Self, He illumines, luminous with His own Light, in identity with Himself, and because He illumines Himself, so too He reflects on His own nature, without His wonder (*camatkāra*) being in any way diminished.

The Kashmiri Śaiva concept of consciousness is clearly more akin in the West to the Christian mystic's understanding of the nature of Deity than to that of consciousness as conceived by most western psychologists and philosophers of mind. Dionysius the Aeropagite talks of God, in the passage cited below, in much the same terms as the Kashmiri Śaivite would about the light of absolute consciousness:

> [God] being One communicates His unity into every part of the world and also unto the Whole, both unto that which is one and that which is many. He is One and unchangeable in a supersential manner being neither a multiplicity of things, nor yet the sum total of such units . . . He is a unity in a manner far different from this . . . He is indivisible plurality, insatiable, yet brimful, producing, perfecting and maintaining all unity and plurality.

The central mystical experience of enlightenment is aptly symbolised by light in most of the numerous forms of mysticism; Deity and all that surrounds the higher reaches of existence are universally symbolised by light. The vision of Light is one of the most characteristic features of higher mystical experiences. When the Kashmiri Śaiva talks of Deity or Reality as Light, he is trying to express his direct experience of the Real; this is more important to the mystic than any concept of reality. The yogi's concern is realisation, not philosophical speculation or theological discussion.

If the mystic is to traverse the boundary between the transitory and the eternal, he must die to the profane condition. He must depart from a world devoid of light to be reborn into the higher, sacred state of enlightenment, into a world he recognises to be full of light. The result is an increase in consciousness; that is, the previous condition is augmented by formerly unconscious contents. The new condition carries with it more insight, which is symbolised by more light. It is a vision of the world radiant with the light and life of the divine reality within all things, and yet beyond them. The most profoundly satisfying experience possible is the recognition that the light of one's own consciousness is all things.

"[This] Bliss", writes Abhinava, "is not like the intoxication of wine or that of riches, nor similar to union with the beloved. The manifestation of the light of consciousness is not like the ray of light from a lamp, sun or moon. When one frees oneself from accumulated multiplicity, the state of bliss is like that of putting down a burden; the manifestation of the Light is like the acquiring of a lost treasure, the domain of universal non-duality."

---

## Page 62: Continuation

This is the central experience upon which the Kashmiri Śaiva bases his understanding of the nature of reality. In the transition from experience (mysticism) to a concept of reality (metaphysics), we can only carry with us ideas symbolic of the original experience. Philosophy, from this point of view, can only serve a descriptive function. It is a 'systematic symbolism' which serves primarily to generate insight into the nature of reality by a process of elevating the philosopher's power of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), allowing him to couple the concept with the experience which lies behind it.

Philosophy is an elaboration of different kinds of spiritual experiences. The abstractions of high-grade metaphysics are based on spiritual experience and derive their whole value from the experiences they symbolise. No metaphysical concept is entirely intelligible without reference to the spirit.

Light (*prakāśa*), Sound (*nāda*), Vibration (*spanda*), Taste (*rasa*) and a host of others all serve this symbolic function in this universe of discourse. Amongst these, Light (*prakāśa*) and Vibration (*spanda*) feature prominently. Light symbolism helps us to grasp the inner relationship between things understood as integral parts of the absolute in static juxtaposition and mutual interpenetration. Vibration (*spanda*) symbolism serves to represent the dynamic, self-regenerative character of the absolute. It symbolises the active participation of the infinite in the finite as the process of its transformation into the finite and the reconversion of the finite into the infinite. The absolute is called 'Light' because it is the universal knowledge of the supreme subject which makes the entire knowable manifest. The way we experience things is therefore only explicable if we agree that the Light which illumines them is somehow both formless and omniform at the same time.

We can explain how consciousness can have these two aspects only if we admit that it is free to be both single and diverse. It cannot be just one or the other for then we would have to posit the existence of a second reality to make up for the deficiency of one or other of these two aspects. Indeed, we cannot say that the Light is either single or diverse for that would imply a division (*bheda*) within it. One way for solving this problem, without recourse to some form of dualism, is to say that unity alone is real and that diversity is merely apparent. All that exists is consciousness which seems to assume diverse forms. This is the Advaitin's view.

The experience we all have to which Abhinava is alluding in this passage is that we perceive various objects in the scan of one perception without it being divided. The same holds true of the universal perception absolute consciousness has of the universe. Accordingly, the Light of Śiva's consciousness is symbolically conceived to be an infinite, perfectly polished (*svaccha*) mirror within which the entire universe is reflected. In this way the Kashmiri Śaiva explains how the one conscious reality can at once be immanent and transcendent without this either compromising its unity or denying the reality of the manifest universe. Consciousness, like a mirror, can reflect objects within itself. It has the power to manifest entities that are separate from it as if they were one with it, without this in any way affecting its nature. Conversely, it also makes manifest these reflected images as if they were distinct from it although they are not. Again, the variety of manifest forms (*ābhāsa*) appear separate from one another, without this compromising the oneness of consciousness, just as happens with the reflections in a mirror. However, in one respect at least, the mirror analogy does not hold good. Reflections in a mirror correspond to outer objects; this is not the case with consciousness. The All (*viśva*) is entirely a reflection (*pratibimbamātra*). From the point of view of consciousness, the original object is as much a reflection as the image reflected in the mirror. Although the universe is like a reflection, there is no object outside the mirror of consciousness that, reflected within it, appears as the universe. Abhinava points out:

> The image reflected [in a mirror] is deposited [there] by the original external object. Now, if this too is a reflected image, what remains of the original object?

This act of reflective awareness is termed '*vimarśa*'. The word is derived from the root '*mṛṣ*' which means to touch, feel, understand, perceive, reflect or examine. This ability to reflect on itself is inherent in the very nature of the light of consciousness; indeed it is its most specific characteristic and the very life of its sentient nature. Deprived of reflective awareness, the light of consciousness would amount to no more than the mere appearing of phenomena unknown to anyone like the light that shines reflected in a common mirror or crystal.

Through this awareness, the Light knows itself to be the sole reality and so rests in itself, but not as does a self-confined, lifeless object. It enjoys perfect freedom and is satisfied (*cariṣṭṭha*) in the knowledge that it is all that exists, be it subject, object or means of knowledge. Self-awareness is God's omniscience, the fullness (*pūrṇatā*) of all-embracing consciousness, its bliss (*ānanda*) or aesthetic rapture (*camatkāra*) that contains within itself the infinite variety of things. By contemplating its own nature, consciousness assumes the form of all the planes of existence from the subtlest to the most gross. The power of reflection is thus the inherent creative freedom of the light of consciousness to either turn in on itself introspectively and be free of its outer forms, or move out of itself to view its outer manifestations. In harmony with the oscillation of awareness between these polarities, the universe of manifestation is incessantly renewed and is the essence of the vitality of its pulsation. The vibration of awareness serves, in short, to account for the manifestation of phenomena without either material cause or essential change in consciousness, and distinguishes the Light as a primary, uncaused principle from its creations.

## Page 71: Continuation

Awareness is the oneness of the unlimited vision of the All. Lack of awareness results in incomplete vision and divides the All into parts, each separately seen as a specific 'this' (*idam*) contrasted and distinguished from all that it is not. Turning away from the unity of self-awareness, we become obsessed with the part and ignore the Whole. But when awareness rests in itself and contemplates its own nature, it sees itself as the pure subject that unfolds as the unity of all things. This awareness (*vimarśa*) can therefore be said to have two aspects:

**Internal.** This is the act of awareness when the light of consciousness rests in itself alone. It is the pure awareness of 'I' (*ahamvimarśa*), devoid of all thought-constructs (*nirvikalpa*), said to be 'total freedom and unsullied wonder'.

**External.** This aspect corresponds to the act of reflection directed away from the subject to the object he perceives as separate from himself. Reality then becomes accessible to discursive representation (*vikalpa*) and amenable to empirical definition.

Awareness serves to relate objectivity with subjectivity in such a way that the object ultimately comes to rest in the self-awareness of the subject. In reality, reflective awareness is always awareness of 'I' (*ahamvimarśa*); it never objectifies even when, in the form of the awareness of 'this' (*idamvimarśa*), it reflects upon the object. The experience we have of things existing outside consciousness is due to a lack of self-awareness. The awareness of the object is never 'out there'; it is registered and known within the subject. All forms of awareness come to rest in the subject.

> Just as every drop of water comes to rest in the ocean, so all acts and cognitions [come to rest] in the Great Lord, the ocean of consciousness. Even a little water on the ground drunk by the sun's rays goes, as rain, to the great ocean. Similarly all knowledge and action in the universe merge in the ocean of Śiva either spontaneously and evidently (*sphuṭam*), by itself or [indirectly] through a series of other [processes].

Individual and universal consciousness are one. The same processes operate in both; the only difference between them is that in the case of individual consciousness these processes are restricted or limited (*saṅkucita*) representations of the maximally expanded (*vikāśa*) operation of universal consciousness. The activity of the mind is that of consciousness itself, or to be more precise, of its reflective awareness, the power of Spanda. Thus, on the individual level, reflective awareness:

> Is the capacity of the Self to know itself in all its purity in the state of perfect freedom from all kinds of affections; to analyse all its states of varying affections, due either to the internal or the external causes; to retain these affections in the form of residual traces (*saṃskāra*); to take out, at will, at any time, anything out of the existing stock of the *saṃskāras* and bring back an old affected state of itself as in the case of remembrance; to create an altogether new state of self-affection by making a judicious selection from the existing stock and displaying the material so selected on the background of the *prakāśa* aspect as at the time of free imagination.

## Page 72: Continuation

Cognition would be impossible if consciousness were incapable of it. This capacity is the reflective awareness it has of itself as pure 'I' consciousness. When it is conditioned by the object of knowledge, which is in its turn conditioned by the forces and laws that govern the physical universe (all of which are aspects of the power of Māyā), it operates as cognition, memory and all the other functions of the mind. This blissful self-awareness (*vimarśa*) is the abiding condition of the subject even while he perceives the world and reacts to it. It is the inner activity of the Spanda principle, which is the inspired wonder (*camatkāra*) of consciousness from which the powers of will, knowledge and action flow out as phases in its vibrating rhythm (*spanda*).

Normally, the individual subject fails to recognise the creative nature of this flow of awareness (*jñānadhārā*) to and from the object in the act of cognition. He is unaware that he fashions from his own consciousness the various forms which populate his objective field of awareness. On the universal level of subjectivity, however, this movement from inner to outer and back is experienced within consciousness as the coming into being and destruction of the entire universe. Consequently, reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is characterized as action (*kriyā*) which is the flux of Becoming, while the Light (*prakāśa*) is knowledge (*jñāna*) or passive Being. In other words, awareness is the creative act of making reality known, while the Light is the actuality of its being known. The latter without the former would be an inactive principle, a state of pure potential that could never actualize into an act of awareness. From this point of view the two aspects of awareness are:

**Karma Vimarśa.** When the act of awareness is directed externally and coincides with the unfolding (*vikāśa*) of the expansion of the universe (*prapañca*) out of the absolute.

**Kriyā Vimarśa.** When this activity is still unlimited and infinite, completely internalized within the absolute as its agency (*kartṛtva*), undisturbed by any goal of action (*kārya*) as the pure vibration or stir (*saṃrambha*) of consciousness.

The Śaiva rejects the Vedāntin's view that knowledge is incommensurable with action. Knowledge and action together constitute the basis of daily life and the life of all living beings. One is never without the other; they function hand in hand. At the universal level, the power of action evolves forms out of the pleroma of consciousness, while the power of knowledge makes them manifest. On the individual level, they represent the objective and subjective poles of all sentient activity. As the inner awareness that 'I am' (*aham*), knowledge is the stable referent of all actions. It persists undivided throughout all action, however diverse. If it did not, then running, for example, would be impossible, nor would we be able to understand a sentence spoken in haste.

### Awareness and the Integral Nature of the Absolute

Although diverse elements may appear within consciousness, they must be distinguished from one another. Individual appearances share a common nature as appearances and so cannot divide themselves off from one another; otherwise the severed elements, disassociated from their essential nature, would not appear at all. Established in its own undifferentiated (*aviśiṣṭa*) nature, the universe would not be a universe unless the light of consciousness itself differentiates the diverse forms it creates by its spontaneous shining. It does this by the various ways in which it reflects upon its own nature. Although the Light is always undivided on the lower level of Māyā as well as on the higher level of pure consciousness, the reflective awareness it has of its own nature is not. Thus while Light expresses the unity of consciousness, awareness, when distinguished from it, expresses the diversity of perceptions. At the microcosmic level we can say:

> The one light of consciousness consists of such types of reflective awareness as: 'this is a jar' and 'this is a cloth'; 'these two are divided from each other and from other subjects as well as from me'.

At the macrocosmic level:

> The Light is the supreme reality (*paramārtha*) that encompasses [the categories] from Earth to Parameśvara, [while] the unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of the reflective awareness of the Heart [of 'I' consciousness] within it, distinguishes between them.

## Page 74: Continuation

This does not mean that *vimarśa* is diverse. Although it is due to the awareness of the unity or relative distinction between the phenomena illumined by the light of consciousness that they are experienced as one or diverse, this is only possible because awareness is the same in both cases. This then is another aspect of the dynamic nature of awareness: it is the 'freedom [of consciousness] to unite, separate and hold things together.' This distinguishes consciousness from inert objects 'devoid of the freedom to conjoin and disjoin.' It is the vibration of consciousness which generates the universe by a process of uniting and dividing the elements contained within it in an undifferentiated state. Thus *vimarśa* is said to operate in four ways: (1) it negates its true nature and (2) identifies with something else, (3) merges both into one and (4) denies both once they have been merged together. These four functions correspond to three levels of reflective awareness, namely, the awareness of the separation, of the holding together and of the union of the manifestations of consciousness. First, by 'negating its true nature and identifying with something else', consciousness, through its power of awareness, freely identifies with the psychophysical organism and denies its true nature as consciousness. The result is the emergence of seemingly individual loci of consciousness distinct from the object and from each other. Second, through the same power of awareness, subject and object are held together and different objects related to one another in a single field of consciousness during the act of cognition. Thirdly, the individual subject and object, together with all diversity, merge in the reflective awareness the light of consciousness has of its nature as the universal subject.

These three levels of awareness correspond to the three-fold appearing of consciousness:

- **Division (*Bheda*)** corresponding to the awareness of separation between objects.

- **Awareness of unity-in-difference (*bhedābheda*)** represented by the means of knowledge which serves as a link between the unity (*abheda*) of the subject and the diversity (*bheda*) of the object.

- **Awareness of the undivided unity (*abheda*)** of all things as the pure subject.

We can understand this movement from two points of view. Firstly, 'vertically' as a movement from the absolute down to its manifestation and back in consonance with the emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) of diversity. This is the pure vibration of its Bliss which contains and pours forth all the powers operating on every plane of existence. Spanda is thus the powerful wave of energy released through the act of self-awareness which carries consciousness from the lower contracted level to the supreme state of expansion, freeing the unawakened from the torments of limitation and awakening them to the fullness of universal consciousness.

The manifestation of the universe and the emergence of Becoming, consisting of both individual subjects and objects, from the inner state of pure Being is equivalent to the emergence of thought in universal consciousness. Thus the movement from inner to outer engenders a split within consciousness between subject and object that gives rise to the perception of relative distinctions. This corresponds to the loss of a direct, thought-free intuition of the essential unity between inner and outer. In the supreme state—that is the 'inner' reality of consciousness—there is no difference between 'inner' and 'outer'. Everything is experienced as part of one, undivided compact mass of consciousness (*samvidghaṭa*). The pure Being (*satṭā*) of universal consciousness assumes the form of Becoming and is involved in time and space only when a contrast appears within it between the perceiver and the perceived:

> The variety of subjects and objects with their characteristic differences is made manifest by the creative power of the Lord, Who knows them.

The creative freedom (*svātantrya*) of the absolute and its deluding power of Māyā are identical. When the power of consciousness is recognised to be the spontaneous expression of the absolute made manifest in the variety of forms it assumes without compromising its essential unity, it is experienced as the pure vibration (*spanda*) of its freedom. If, however, the cosmic outpouring (*viśvollāsa*) of consciousness is felt to consist of diverse and conflicting elements, the same power is called Māyā. The field of operation of the freedom of the absolute is the kingdom of universal consciousness, while that of its power of Māyā is the world of trans-migratory existence. The difference between them is based on the degree of insight we have into the nature of reality. Due to this power the object appears to be projected outside the subject even though it is always manifest within it and is the inner reality of the object. The creation of diversity is accordingly defined as 'the projection (*kṣepa*) of one's own nature into the Self from the Self'. Abhinava explains:

> Creation is to make that which shines within, externally manifest while it still preserves its original internal nature. Therefore [the object] must be made manifest by that in relation to which it is said to be internal and which makes the internal externally manifest.

Conversely, the moment-to-moment destruction of the objective content of consciousness occurs by a reversal of the movement from inner to outer. The object, in other words, is never destroyed, but merely withdrawn into the inner reality of the subject. The Spanda teachings agree with the Buddhist doctrine of momentariness only insofar as it applies to outer objectivity.

---

## Page 80: Continuation

Although perception and every phenomenal occurrence can be analysed into a series of moments (*kṣaṇa*), daily life cannot entirely be understood in terms of such moment-units. Change is an activity within the absolute which can only be properly understood in terms of conscious action and not as a mechanical process. Each act is part of a single continuous motion which proceeds from the agent—the pure Being of introverted consciousness—to its final completion in the result, which is the object or deed (*kārya*). The outer reality of Becoming is the effect which emerges from the cause, the inner reality of Being, just as action emerges from the agent. It is a wave of activity which rises out of the infinite potential of the agent. Every event is a part of the greater rhythm of the total, cosmic event. Every object is part of the universal object and every subject shares in the agency of the universal subject. Kṣemarāja writes:

> Hence the Lord creates and destroys only the objective aspect of the perceiver, i.e., the body, etc., but not the subjective aspect which is the light of 'I' consciousness because although embodied, the subject is, in reality, one with the Lord. Thus of the two—subject and object—the latter is perishable while the former is the freedom of consciousness and immortal. For even when the world is emanated and absorbed [the subject] does not waver from his true nature. If he were to do so, the emanation and absorption of the world would not be manifest [for there would be none to perceive it].

The inner is the domain of Being, where the subject's power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) operates within itself, while the outer is the domain of the subject's power of action (*kriyāśakti*). Knowledge turns into action and action leads to knowledge. Thus every individual phenomenon has two aspects: its outer form and its inner nature. Its outer form is apparent to us as the manner in which it behaves, its properties and pragmatic efficacy (*arthakriyā*). This aspect differentiates each individual object from other objects and renders it accessible to conceptual representation (*savikalpa*). Its inner nature the Kashmiri Śaiva equates with its pure Being as an appearance (*ābhāsa*) within universal consciousness as 'one with' pure 'I-ness' and hence inaccessible to conceptual representation (*nirvikalpa*). Thus the movement from Being to Becoming is essentially an act of perception. Perception is the connecting link between the outer manifest form of the object and its inner nature. The movement of awareness from inner to outer is equivalent to a movement from an awareness of the unity of the inner nature of all things to the diversity of their outer forms. The activity of consciousness gives rise to diversity in this sense alone.

---

## Page 81: Continuation

Although it would not be wrong to say that the absolute is in a constant state of transformation or is full of vibration—Spanda—from another point of view we could say that no change or movement occurs in the absolute at all. Movement (*saṃrambha*) and rest (*viśrānti*) in the absolute presuppose one another. The freedom (*svātantrya*) of consciousness to do what seems, according to reason, to be impossible explains how the absolute can at once be motionless and yet full of activity. Abhinava explains:

> By 'vibration' (*spanda*) [we mean] subtle movement. It is subtle [in the sense that] although it moves not, it manifests as motion. The light of consciousness is not at all separate [from manifestation] yet it appears to be so. Thus, that which is immobile, associated with the variety of manifestation, manifests [as movement].

Motion normally implies a movement between two separate points, which entails the existence of at least two distinct entities between which motion can occur. But as all things are equally consciousness there are no two such distinct realities between which motion, as we understand it, can take place. Abhinava explains that Spanda—the pulsation of consciousness—is defined as a 'subtle movement' (*kiñcitkācalana*) because 'if that movement [were] to entail motion towards another entity, it would not be 'subtle' [but merely gross motion]; if not, [on the other hand], it is not motion at all.'

The cosmic process consists of a cyclic series of creations and destructions which follow one another like buckets fixed on a water-wheel. Although change is manifest through this process, and change is the basis of time, the pulsation of the absolute is a movement outside the confines of time. Śiva is eternally engaged in all the phases of the creative act simultaneously and yet performs them one after another. So Utpaladeva sings of Śiva's glory thus:

The work matters here because it lets the Buddhist analysis of selfing enter a clinical and interpersonal field: aggregates, dependent arising, emptiness, need, desire, and the therapeutic relation cease to be separable theoretical topics and become different views of how a self-world is formed, defended, loosened, and re-related. The second, gathered here from the thesis at pp. 112–13, passes through Steven Gans's reading of Emmanuel Levinas. Egoic interiority converts what is “not me” into what is “for me”; a world and its others are represented, penetrated, and managed within an economy of need. Levinas's face-to-face interrupts that economy because the Other exceeds the idea, image, or use through which the ego tries to make the encounter commensurate with its powers. Gans joins that interruption to psychotherapy by describing a movement from egoic need toward interpersonal desire. Watson then places this Levinasian movement beside Buddhist discourse. Her immediate comparison turns upon the separately fabricated self and the defensive objectification that follows from its insecurity. #### 3.1 Dissociation, tattvic contraction, and the slash — one event under the paśu

Frank's point: Kastrup's dissociation, the Śaiva tattvic contraction, and the slash describe the same thing; they are closer than any comparative hedging suggests; and the Śaiva "contraction" is not "merely" anything — it is the positive, self-imposed `saṃkoca` in which consciousness contracts into the limited subject. The framing already in house is the paśu: the contracted subject-position, the specific horizonal boundary of a given objective internality (Frank's own language in the Watson notes). The background metaphor that lets all three stand in proper relation is the cosmos as the dream or simulation of the divine mind; Māyā is that dream — what Frank calls the "Dreamcode" or "Dream-machine" — and the metaphors of life as illusion, dream, simulation, and game all resolve through the same mechanism: an internal difference appearing as external separation (Argument 13), the horizon that gives by withholding (the 07–09 August run), the membrane between simulated and real that perforates (Simulation concept).

Register discipline preserved: Kastrup's analytic idealism is a contemporary philosophical formalisation of the order of dependence (mind/consciousness first); Trika gives the internally differentiated anatomy (prakāśa–vimarśa–māyā, kañcukas, antaḥkaraṇa, paśu); the slash is the operation itself (`0/1 = 1/0`, AND/OR). They are one event, not three similar metaphors — but each keeps its own vocabulary, source, and burden of warrant.

#### 3.2 Māyā as the dream — Dreamcode / Dream-machine

The veiling structure is a computational structure. Māyā is the horizonalisation of the prakāśa–vimarśa relation: the point where "this can appear while that remains hidden" becomes possible; Mahāmāyā is still Śakti, the power that hides being the same power that reveals and measures. The kañcukas give the horizon its coordinates (time, place/order, limited knowledge, limited efficacy, incompletion/desire); Puruṣa is the point for which the coordinate patch is mine; Prakṛti is the structured recurrence available within the finite field. The "dream" name is exact in the state-structure register: dream proves that objective cannot mean externally material — the foundation of objective internality — and the sleeper's forgetting that one sleeps is what lets the dream register as real (Frank's Draft-3 image). "Dreamcode"/"Dream-machine" names the rule-bound, bounded, executable world through which a local agent can perceive and act: everyday Māyā is the measured, bounded, executable world (Computational Process Ontology), and the Simulation concept already carries the real-to-sim-to-real relays and the perforating membrane.

The naming is open: "Dreamcode" and "Dream-machine" are Frank's live vocabulary, not yet canonical; they are recorded here as candidates pending his Neumann–Māyā notes.

#### 3.3 Faggin, the flip-switch, and the superposition — correction: not `0/0`

Faggin as father of the microprocessor becomes a central technical-register entry. The `0/1` of binary, read as a flip-switch, implies that the logic it actually runs is `(-1)/(+1)`: two states are signed poles around the axis, with zero as the retained centre of tension and connection — polar dia-ballein, not yet the ground–mark relation. That gives the headroom for the claim of returning to `0/1` as paradoxical: after the switch has fallen into signed counter-position, the return to `0/1` is the slash that holds both orientations at once — `(0/1)/(1/0)`, the AND/OR co-presence of ground and mark, "simultaneous relational presence, not probabilistic blur or fusion" (§2 · #2; Argument 03). **This is the superposition.**

**Correction recorded:** the superposition is not `0/0`. `0/0 = %` is indeterminate potency — "every possible ratio held at once," maximal capacity — a different operation. The likely source of the slip is the core-theorem proportional table's phrase "the superposition of all proportions" for `%`; that phrase is potency-language, not the superpositional logic. The house superpositional logic is sym-ballein: `(0/1)/(1/0)`, ground and manifestation as inverse orientations of one appearing-act. Quantum state space enters later as an exact formal neighbour (CP¹/Bloch-sphere geometry at §3 · #28), never as the origin of the ontology.

### 2. Bimba and pratibimba: ontological priority and epistemic recovery

**Bimba is the Original.** It names the originary form or order whose reflections disclose it without dividing or diminishing it. **Pratibimba is the reflection**, the image in which that Original appears under another condition, surface, lens, angle, or register. A pratibimba depends upon its Bimba, bears its order, and displays it partially. Bimba does not become a picture produced by the reflective process.

This relation carries a decisive asymmetry. Bimba is prior in being and later in recognition. Pratibimbas are encountered as determinate appearances; their recurrent proportions, inversions, agreements, distortions, and phase-relations allow the Original order to be recognised through them. The Original is therefore inferred or re-cognised from the lawful differentiation of its images while remaining the condition from which their law proceeds. Pratyabhijñā gives this return its proper verb: the source is recognised through the forms in which it had never ceased to be active.

The Śaiva mirror argument deepens the point. The universe appears as reflection within Consciousness, while no external original stands outside the mirror of Consciousness waiting to be copied. In Abhinavagupta's argument as transmitted by Dyczkowski, ordinary convention can call the appearing world “original” if it wishes; the wise attend to the operative facts. Consciousness generates and hosts the reflections within itself. The Bimba is therefore originary Consciousness and its ordering power, while its pratibimbas are real displays within that field rather than replicas of a separately existing exterior object.

### 5. Jung: individuation as becoming indivisible

It supplies no warrant for weakening the proposition, placing a modal around it, or treating it as Frank's uncertain paraphrase.

“Individual” must therefore be heard through its negative interior: *in-dividual*, that which has become incapable of being divided without losing the relation that makes it whole. Individuation cannot culminate in the ego's successful separation from the agencies, oppositions, unconscious formations, wounds, and unchosen conditions through which it exists. It brings those differentiated powers into a relation whose wholeness no longer depends upon their exclusion.

The Self gives this indivisibility its psychic horizon. Complexes, archetypal figures, shadow, anima or animus, ego, body, personal history, and collective inheritance remain differentiated. Their relation to the Self prevents any one local agency from claiming to be the whole. The indivisible psyche carries plurality without dismemberment and unity without absorption.

Close or remove the handle and the topology changes. Count only the positive material of the surface while excluding the hole, and the count omits the condition that makes this surface the surface it is.

The torus refuses that settlement. Its “nothing” occupies the centre of its form without becoming a thing; the entire surface bends, joins, and circulates in dependence upon that unfilled place. The hole is absent as content and present as topology.
